definition.name: NXdose

symbol.name: n_points
symbol.doc: Number of points in the dose trajectory series

symbol.name: n_resolutions
symbol.doc: Number of resolution shells for relative diffraction efficiency

definition.doc: Absorbed radiation dose and radiation damage modeling on the sample. Applicable across macromolecular crystallography (MX), BioSAXS, cryo-tomography, and serial imaging.

field.name: average_absorbed_dose
field.doc: Mean absorbed dose across the illuminated sample volume (typically in Gy or MGy).

field.name: max_absorbed_dose
field.doc: Peak absorbed dose in the highest-dose voxel (typically in Gy or MGy), useful as a conservative safety threshold.

field.name: dose_rate
field.doc: Instantaneous or average absorbed dose rate (typically in Gy/s or MGy/s).

field.name: dose_target
field.doc:
The dose ceiling this measurement was planned against, chosen before the data were collected (typically in Gy or MGy).
This is a statement of intent rather than a property of the sample: it records the budget the exposure was designed to satisfy, and so explains why the exposure was what it was. It may be a general limit, or chosen per specimen from the diffracting power or signal expected of it, a specimen expected to perform poorly being given a larger budget than one with more to lose.
Distinct from ``dose_threshold``. A measurement may be planned well below a damage threshold, or knowingly exceed one.

field.name: dose_threshold
field.doc:
The dose at which radiation damage becomes significant (typically in Gy or MGy).
In macromolecular crystallography this may be a general experimental limit such as the Garman limit (30 MGy for cryo-cooled crystals) or the Henderson limit (20 MGy). In BioSAXS it may be the onset of radiation-induced aggregation. It may also be a value determined for this specimen by analysis of an earlier measurement, which is generally not available while the measurement being described is still running.
Distinct from ``dose_target``, which records the ceiling a measurement was planned against rather than where damage is expected.

field.name: absorbed_dose_series
field.doc: Accumulated absorbed dose trajectory over time/frames.

field.name: time
field.doc:
Time coordinate corresponding to each point in the series.
The times are relative to the ``start`` attribute and in the units given by the ``units`` attribute, following the same convention as :ref:`NXlog`. The ``scaling_factor``, when present, has to be applied to the values in order to arrive at the units specified in the ``units`` attribute.
Either this field or ``angle`` may be used as the coordinate of the series, depending on which is the natural independent variable of the measurement. A rotation experiment is normally indexed by ``angle``.

field.name: frame_number
field.doc: Frame or image sequence index corresponding to each trajectory point. Optional and unnecessary if the series is sequential and continuous with image frames, but useful if the series is sampled on a different grid or if frames are discontinuous.

field.name: diffraction_weighted_dose
field.doc: Diffraction-weighted dose (DWD) for the whole wedge (typically in Gy or MGy). Weights local absorbed dose by where diffraction actually originates.

field.name: diffraction_weighted_dose_series
field.doc: Accumulated diffraction-weighted dose trajectory per image or rotation step.

field.name: angle
field.doc: Goniometer rotation angle corresponding to each trajectory point.

field.name: relative_diffraction_efficiency
field.doc: Predicted survival fraction of diffraction intensity (0.0 to 1.0) as a function of trajectory point and resolution shell.

field.name: resolution
field.doc: Resolution shells corresponding to the columns of ``relative_diffraction_efficiency``, given as d-spacing (e.g. [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] Angstroms).

field.name: calculation_method
field.doc: Method used to obtain dose values.

field.name: composition_source
field.doc:
Provenance of the sample composition that the absorbed dose was computed from.
Absorbed dose depends on the elemental composition of the sample through its X-ray absorption coefficient, and that composition is often not known at the time the dose is calculated. A dose computed from a stand-in composition is not comparable with one computed from the real composition of the sample, and an archived value that does not say which was used cannot be interpreted afterwards. This field records that distinction; ``input_parameters`` may carry the detail.
* ``supplied``: the composition was provided for this specific sample, for example as a sequence, a unit cell or a declared heavy-atom content. * ``derived``: part or all of the composition was inferred from other information about this specific sample, for example from the unit cell contents or from analysis of a sequence. Use this where some components were provided and others inferred, which is the common case: it records that an inference the reader may wish to check was involved. * ``assumed``: a standard or default composition was used in place of an unknown one. The dose is then a scale factor for a typical specimen rather than a statement about this sample. The assumed composition itself should be recorded in ``input_parameters``, since a reader cannot otherwise tell which standard was used or correct for it later. * ``unknown``: the provenance of the composition was not recorded.

field.name: program
field.doc: Name and version of the program used to calculate dose (e.g. "RADDOSE-3D 4.0 via microdose").

field.name: input_parameters
field.doc:
A record of the inputs the dose was computed from, sufficient to interpret or reproduce the calculation afterwards. Typically the engine and its version, the sample composition actually used, and the beam conditions assumed.
Record the composition that the absorption calculation consumed: the elemental content and the number of residues or monomer units. This is both the reproducible record, being what determines the absorption coefficient, and a safe one. Sample composition may be commercially or personally sensitive, and a file written at a facility is frequently archived or published later, but an elemental composition cannot be read back as the identity of the specimen.
A biological sequence is therefore not required and is discouraged here: what the absorption calculation takes from one is its elemental content, and recording that instead loses no ability to reproduce the dose. Where a sequence was used and a link back to it is wanted, a checksum of it may be given in addition to the composition, never in place of it.
